To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the resting state network is altered after consumption of high caloric food.
high-caloric food consumption induces significant connectivity changes in resting state fMRI that can be detected using a support vector machine and graph theoretical analysis.
the brain networks are modulated by high-calorie food, and that this is associated with BMI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of how the brain adapts to food stimuli.
the mechanisms of how the brain adapts to high vs. low-calorie food stimulation and the potential role of BMI on this process.
how food stimuli can induce changes in the human brain, and the possible role of these changes in the development of non-homeostatic eating behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the consumption of high-caloric food can induce significant changes on resting state networks, and these changes can be accurately classified with graph theoretical analysis and support vector machines.
the brain is capable of adapting to food intake and this can be detected using functional connectivity and graph theory.
snack foods can induce significant resting-state network changes in healthy human subjects, which can be detected using machine learning algorithms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain networks can adapt quickly to the food stimulation and the BMI may be an important biomarker for this response.
high caloric food consumption induces a change in brain connectivity and that the change is associated with BMI.
the brain is capable of adapting to short time exposures to different types of food, and that these adaptations can be used as a biomarker to classify between different types of food.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the resting state functional connectivity can be used to identify food biomarkers, which can be further used to understand how food stimuli affect brain activity.
resting state networks can be modulated by food stimuli, which may provide a mechanism by which food can induce non-homeostasis feeding behavior.
the resting state networks can be modulated by the consumption of different food items, which can potentially be used to develop biomarkers for non-homeostatic eating.
